Stage 3 · Grammar

something, anywhere, nobody

Four beginnings, three endings, and one rule that decides between them.

Read these four sentences from the recording.
  • Manga cafes are a good choice if you’re looking for somewhere cheap to spend the night.
  • I haven’t seen anything like this before!
  • Nobody’s serving food.
  • Everyone leaves their shoes outside the room.
One or more of the sentences is negative. Which beginning does it use?
Choose the beginning, then choose the ending
Beginning— one / — body (a person)— thing— where (a place)
some- in positive sentencesSomeone is waiting.I need something to eat.Somewhere cheap to sleep.
any- in negatives and questionsI didn’t see anyone.Is there anything to eat?We didn’t go anywhere.
no- = a negative on its ownNobody is serving food.There is nothing to do.Nowhere is open.
every- = all of themEveryone leaves their shoes.Try everything once.Manga cafes are everywhere.
The verb after italways singular: everyone is here, nothing works — not everyone are
Adjective after itthe adjective comes after, not before: somewhere cheap, something hot — not cheap somewhere
any- in a positive sentencemeans it does not matter which: Sit anywhere.  Ask anyone — they all know.

THE RULE. Some- in positive sentences, any- in negatives and questions. No- is already negative, so the verb stays positive.

FORM. The verb after one of these words is always singular: everybody knows, nothing is open.

The mistake to watch: I didn’t see nobody. One negative is enough — I didn’t see anybody or I saw nobody.

THE RULE. Use some- in positive sentences: There is something in my bag. Use any- in negatives and questions: Is there anything in my bag? / There isn’t anything in my bag.

NO- IS ALREADY NEGATIVE. There is nothing in my bag means the same as There isn’t anything in my bag. Use one negative, not two.

SINGULAR VERB. Everyone is here. Nobody knows. Nothing works. The word looks plural but the verb is singular. To refer back to it, English uses their: Everyone leaves their shoes outside.

WORD ORDER. The adjective goes after: somewhere hot, something cheap, nothing interesting.

Two mistakes to watch: I didn’t see nobody (two negatives), and everyone are ready (plural verb).

You will meet these words again in Lesson 21, where you use them to describe what is wrong with a hotel room.

Full grammar reference — Indefinite pronouns

Form

Peoplesomebody / someone · anybody · nobody · everybody
Thingssomething · anything · nothing · everything
Placessomewhere · anywhere · nowhere · everywhere
With an adjectivethe adjective comes after: somewhere hot · nothing interesting
Verb formthey all take a singular verb: Everybody is here.

When and why we use it

  • Some- is used in positive sentences; any- in negatives and most questions.
  • Any- in a positive sentence means ‘it does not matter which’: You can sit anywhere.
  • No- words are already negative, so the verb stays positive: Nobody came.
  • Some- appears in a question when you offer or expect ‘yes’: Would you like something to drink?

Signal words

somewhere hot · nothing to do · anywhere near · everyone I know

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • Nobody didn’t come. → Nobody came.One negative is enough.
  • There was nothing interesting to do anywhere. → correctThis one is right — any- after a negative.
  • Everybody are here. → Everybody is here.Singular verb.
  • I want to go hot somewhere. → I want to go somewhere hot.The adjective follows the pronoun.

Don’t confuse it with

somebody and someone mean exactly the same; so do somebody’s partners in every row.
